content: Flexion, in anatomical terms, refers to a movement that occurs when the angle of a joint decreases. This movement is facilitated by the coordinated action of the skeletal system, which includes bones, cartilage, and ligaments, and the muscular system, which comprises muscles and tendons. For instance, flexion of the elbow occurs when the hand is brought closer to the shoulder. Similarly, the trunk can be flexed forward toward the legs, or the neck can be flexed downward toward the chest. The opposite movement to flexion is known as extension, which involves straightening the joint and increasing the angle between the bones. Flexion specifically reduces the angle between the bones of a limb at a joint, while extension increases it. These movements occur in the forward and backward directions, not in the side-to-side direction, which is instead described by the term abduction. Active range of motion exercises often include movements such as flexion and extension. These exercises are commonly prescribed following an injury or surgical procedure. Initially, they are performed under the guidance of a physical therapist or nurse, but they may later be continued independently by the patient. During the healing process, it is critical to avoid forcing the limb into extreme flexion or extension positions, as this can place undue stress on the affected area and potentially lead to re-injury.
